claims.text: The starting composite contains tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten ligaments in a continuous copper matrix.
The W–Cu interface is prone to void formation and phase separation under high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
The tungsten component should be pre-coated with a thin nickel layer before composite consolidation.
The nickel coating forms a graded interfacial layer between tungsten and copper.
The nickel-derived interfacial layer improves bonding between tungsten and copper.
The nickel layer reduces W–Cu interfacial energy.
The nickel layer enhances wettability at the W–Cu interface.
Reduced interfacial energy and enhanced wettability mitigate local chemical-potential gradients.
Local chemical-potential gradients drive phase separation and interfacial void nucleation.
Mitigating phase separation and void nucleation stabilizes the interface and preserves thermally conductive pathways.
After thermal cycling and irradiation, Ni-pre-coated W–Cu will have a lower interfacial void density than untreated W–Cu.
After thermal cycling and irradiation, Ni-pre-coated W–Cu will exhibit less phase separation than untreated W–Cu.
Ni-pre-coated W–Cu will retain or modestly increase effective thermal conductivity relative to untreated W–Cu after exposure.
Untreated W–Cu composites typically develop interfacial voids and phase separation under comparable operating conditions.
Interfacial void formation and phase separation degrade the thermal conductivity of untreated W–Cu composites.
The intervention is expected to work under service conditions typical of high-heat-flux plasma-facing components and copper-cooling joints.
The efficacy of the nickel interlayer may diminish at irradiation doses or temperatures well beyond the component design window.
The expected thermal-conductivity improvement is on the order of several percent.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity response depends on processing details and service conditions.
